analysis.one_liner: Forces faster retrofit of aging oil tank cars plus speed limits, inspections, and spill plans for oil trains.
analysis.headline: The oil train safety bill picked up 6 cosponsors, never got a committee vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required railroads to retrofit or retire older DOT-111 and unjacketed CPC-1232 tank cars on faster deadlines than federal rules allowed, and capped trains carrying those cars at 40 mph through any county with more than 20 people per square mile. It also would have added track inspections, required a crash-avoidance system called positive train control on lines carrying crude oil and ethanol by December 2018, and made railroads maintain oil spill response plans. Railroads would have had to let employees anonymously report safety problems and hand detailed derailment information to federal and county emergency officials within minutes of a crash.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live along rail lines carrying oil, especially in populated counties, who would face less risk from older, crash-prone tank cars moving at high speed. First responders would get detailed information about what derailed within 90 minutes, including safety data sheets for the chemicals aboard. Railroad employees would gain an anonymous system for reporting unsafe conditions without fear of retaliation.

how_it_helps.text: Phases out or forces retrofit of older DOT-111 and unjacketed CPC-1232 tank cars to the tougher DOT-117 standard on firm deadlines between 2017 and 2020, faster than general federal requirements allowed

Caps at 40 mph any train of more than 10 cars that includes a non-retrofitted DOT-111 or unjacketed CPC-1232 tank car traveling through a county with population density above 20 people per square mile

Requires two extra internal-rail-defect inspections per 40 million gross tons and four track geometry inspections a year on main lines carrying high-hazard flammable trains, and requires positive train control — a system that can automatically stop a train before a collision — on every rail line carrying crude oil or ethanol by December 1, 2018
Requires comprehensive oil spill response plans for carriers of crude and petroleum, with an FRA audit program to verify the plans cover worst-case discharges

Lets railroad employees anonymously report unsafe conditions, and requires carriers to give the FRA and the county emergency contact detailed derailment information immediately, including chemical safety data sheets and, within 90 minutes, the identities of the companies that extracted, tested, and shipped the oil

analysis.who_pays: Freight railroads, which would bear the retrofit deadlines, 40 mph speed caps, added inspections, extended positive train control costs, and new reporting systems. The costs would flow through to oil producers and other shippers who rely on rail to move crude, and to tank car owners facing write-downs on older fleets. Consumers could see some of it in fuel and shipping costs.

drawbacks.text: The retrofit deadlines, 40 mph speed caps, added inspections, and extending positive train control to crude and ethanol lines by December 2018 would have imposed significant compliance costs on railroads and shippers, some of which would likely reach consumers through freight rates

The Department of Transportation had just issued its May 2015 final rule creating the DOT-117 standard with its own phase-out schedule, so the bill's statutory deadlines overlapped and partially conflicted with a brand-new regulation — a fair objection that Congress should let the expert agency's rule work before locking in stricter dates
A national maximum volatility standard for crude would have restricted which oil could move by rail or barge at all, a real economic constraint on producers even if justified by fire risk

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case was real: older DOT-111 cars had been involved in catastrophic oil train derailments, and quick notification to county emergency officials addresses a genuine gap for first responders. The compliance costs were also real but one-time and concentrated in an industry that had just absorbed a federal safety rule covering much of the same ground. The bill's main design weakness was piling statutory deadlines on top of a freshly issued regulation rather than letting the rule play out. On balance, the protections for populated communities and first responders outweighed the cost to carriers and shippers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee never took the bill up after it was referred, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Schumer introduced the bill on May 22, 2015, joined by Democratic senators Durbin, Gillibrand, Boxer, and Feinstein as original cosponsors
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced
No further action of any kind appears in the record — no markup, no hearing, no vote — through the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017
The bill arrived just as the Department of Transportation was finalizing its own May 2015 rule adopting the DOT-117 tank car standard, but with slower phase-out deadlines than this bill proposed

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Freight railroads and crude oil shippers were better off: they avoided faster retrofit deadlines, the 40 mph cap through populated counties, expanded inspections, and an extended positive train control mandate. Communities along oil train routes never received the added protections, and first responders never got the rapid derailment disclosure rules.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its promotion

for.name: Sens. Durbin, Gillibrand, Boxer, and Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (Chair John Thune)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, hearing, or vote — for the remaining year and a half of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill; its seven supporters were all Democrats plus one Independent, and the Republican-chaired Commerce Committee never brought it to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed faster tank car retrofit deadlines, 40 mph speed limits through populated counties, extra track inspections, positive train control on crude and ethanol lines by December 2018, spill response plans, and new reporting duties. Railroads' cost savings from avoiding these mandates came at the expense of safety protections for the communities their trains pass through.

industries.industry: Crude oil producers and rail shippers
industries.note: A national maximum volatility standard and the accelerated phase-out of older tank cars would have raised the cost of moving crude by rail and restricted which oil could ship. The industry's preference for the slower federal phase-out left residents near rail lines with older cars on the tracks longer.

Retrofit mandates create paid work for tank car builders and shops, but owners of legacy DOT-111 fleets face write-downs and retrofit bills on cars that the bill would have retired or rebuilt faster than the federal rule required.
